notes.meaning: Ishmael, who belonged to the royal family of Judah, arrived at Mizpah with ten men to visit Gedaliah. Gedaliah welcomed them warmly and shared a meal with them. In biblical culture, eating together was a solemn sign of peace and friendship, which made Ishmael's secret plan an awful betrayal.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that several years passed between the fall of Jerusalem and Gedaliah's assassination, rather than just two or three months.

notes.meaning: During or right after the meal, Ishmael and his ten men drew their swords and murdered Gedaliah. They killed the very leader the king of Babylon had placed in charge to protect and govern the surviving remnant. Their violent act shattered the peaceful community Gedaliah had worked to build.

Ishmael and his men went on to kill all the Judean officials and soldiers stationed with Gedaliah, along with the Babylonian guards who were there. This slaughter was done to prevent any immediate resistance or revenge. Ishmael acted with ruthless speed so no one could stop him.

Two days after the murder of Gedaliah, people outside Mizpah still knew nothing about it. Ishmael kept the city locked down so news would not spread to the surrounding towns. This silence set the stage for Ishmael to trap his next group of victims.

Eighty men from northern towns arrived carrying grain offerings and incense, heading toward the ruined house of the Lord to pray. They had shaved their beards, torn their clothes, and cut their skin as traditional signs of intense mourning over Jerusalem's destruction. Even though the temple had been burned, these devout men still sought God's mercy at the holy site.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that ancient Greek manuscripts read 'Salem' instead of 'Shiloh,' while others propose that these worshippers were traveling to an altar temporarily set up at Mizpah.

notes.meaning: Ishmael walked out from Mizpah to meet the pilgrims, pretending to weep so he would look like a fellow mourner. He invited them to enter the city to meet Gedaliah, completely hiding the fact that he had already killed the governor. His false tears and friendly words were designed to lead them straight into an ambush.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the ancient Greek translation describes the visiting pilgrims as weeping rather than Ishmael.

notes.meaning: Once the unsuspecting pilgrims walked inside Mizpah, Ishmael and his men slaughtered seventy of them. They tossed the dead bodies into a large underground cistern to hide what they had done. This was an act of senseless cruelty against harmless worshippers.

Ten of the men saved their lives by bargaining with Ishmael. They told him they had secret underground stores of wheat, barley, olive oil, and honey hidden in the fields. Because Ishmael was greedy and needed food for his followers, he spared these ten men to secure the hidden goods.

The cistern Ishmael used as a mass grave was built centuries earlier by King Asa of Judah to store water during a war with King Baasha of Israel. Ishmael filled this large reservoir with the bodies of the pilgrims and Gedaliah's supporters. A place originally designed to preserve life during a siege was turned into a pit of death.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars prefer the ancient Greek reading that describes the pit simply as a 'great cistern,' or understand the Hebrew phrase to mean Ishmael used Gedaliah's name as a trap.

notes.meaning: Ishmael took captive the remaining people of Mizpah, including the royal princesses who had been entrusted to Gedaliah's care. He began marching them eastward toward the land of Ammon. He intended to give or sell these captives to the Ammonite king who had backed his conspiracy.

Johanan and the other Judean army captains soon heard about the terrible crimes Ishmael had committed at Mizpah. They had warned Gedaliah earlier about this very danger, and now their warnings had come true. They quickly mobilized their forces to avenge the innocent and save the survivors.

Johanan and his commanders gathered all their soldiers and set out to pursue Ishmael. They caught up with him at the great pool of Gibeon, just a short distance from Mizpah. Ishmael had halted near this large water reservoir on his way to Ammon, giving the rescue party time to corner him.

When the captives with Ishmael saw Johanan and the army commanders coming toward them, they were filled with joy. They were being taken against their will and desperately wanted rescue from Ishmael's brutality. The arrival of the Judean troops brought them immediate relief and hope.

All the captives whom Ishmael had dragged from Mizpah turned their backs on him and ran to join Johanan. Ishmael lost all control over the people in a single moment. Without support from the people, his tyrannical hold completely collapsed.

Realizing he was outnumbered and abandoned by his captives, Ishmael fled for his life with only eight men. Since he originally arrived with ten followers, two of his men had likely been killed in the conflict. He managed to cross over the border to Ammon, escaping human justice for a season.

Johanan and his fellow officers gathered the whole group of survivors whom they had rescued at Gibeon. This remnant included soldiers, women, children, and palace court officials who had survived the slaughter at Mizpah. Johanan stepped forward as their protector and leader, though the community was now uprooted and shaken.

Johanan led the entire company south past Jerusalem and stopped at an inn near Bethlehem called Geruth Chimham. This place was connected to Chimham, the son of Barzillai, whom King David had rewarded long before. Johanan set up camp there as a temporary resting stop while preparing to take everyone down to Egypt.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that early translations read this place name as a sheepfold or shelter for flocks rather than a lodging inn for travelers.

notes.meaning: Johanan and the leaders decided to flee to Egypt because they were terrified of the Babylonians. They feared the Babylonian king would send an army to punish the whole remnant because the appointed governor, Gedaliah, had been murdered on Judean soil. Fear of human wrath led them to look for safety in Egypt rather than trusting in God's protection.
